text: JAMM 448: Law of Mass Media Spring 2019 Professor: Dr. Katie Blevins Email: katieblevins@uidaho.edu (please put JAMM 448 in the subject line of your email) Phone: 885-8873 Office: 342A Administration Building Office Hours: T/R: 10 am- 1 pm, and by appointment Class: T/R 2:00-3:15 pm, Admin 227 Course Description Welcome to the Law of Mass Media! This course will introduce you to legal decisions as well as government and industry policies that impact media and media professionals. While this course will not prepare you to start your own legal practice (or expect you to want to!), it will, however, prepare you to not be sued. You will be able to identify legal problems and solutions associated with media law, whether you plan to become a journalist, a media professional or even more important perhaps, an engaged citizen. No prior legal background is necessary. Law of Mass Media is a senior course for all (accredited) majors in the School of Journalism and Mass Media. This class helps you draw on skills you have acquired in our program (journalism, advertising, public relations, and broadcasting & digital media), while sharpening the skills essential for media practitioners: research, critical analysis, and clear and effective communication. Course Objectives After completing this course, you will be able to: - Recognize, recall, and retrieve information relevant to specific areas of media law, including statutes and cases. - Differentiate and discuss specific areas of media law, and relevant statutes and cases. - Interpret and solve hypothetical legal problems based on your foundation of Knowledge and Comprehension.  - Rewrite and explain primary legal documents to create new meaning and structure from a close reading of the texts.  - Finally, assess and assign value to the knowledge and skills gained in this class in relation to professional career tracks. Learning Outcomes To accomplish these goals, JAMM 448 requires students to analyze actual cases, research current media law debates, and apply media law principles to factual scenarios and controversies. While most debates in media law have no clear “right” or “wrong” answer, this course is designed to help students adopt a critical/analytical approach to problem solving. This course also integrates the five University of Idaho learning outcomes: 1. Learn and integrate. 2. Think and create. 3. Communicate. 4. Practice citizenship. 5. Clarify purpose and perspective. Required Texts & Readings Pember, Don R. and Clay Calvert, Mass Media Law. Boston: McGraw-Hill, 20th Edition. Since the law is constantly updating and changing, you are required to have the current edition of this textbook. You must complete and be prepared to discuss all assigned readings for the date noted in this syllabus. Material from the book will appear on tests even if not covered in class. Course Requirements: Your grade in this course will be based on the items listed below. The grading breakdown is as follows: Test #1 1/31 15% (150 points) Test #2 2/28 15% (150 points) Test #3 4/4 15% (150 points) Paper #1: Case Problem 4/11 10% (100 points) Test #4 5/2 15% (150 points) Paper #2: Reflective Essay 5/8 10% (100 points) Homework and In-Class Assignments Ongoing 10% (100 points) Attendance Ongoing 10% (100 points) Please note that all assignments are graded out of 100% and then weighted to reflect the points above. So a test will be graded out of 100% but worth 15%/150 points of your total grade. So if you receive a 100% on your test, you will see 150 points on BB Learn. The university’s standard grading scale will be applied: A = 90-100%/900-1000 points, B = 80-89%/800-899 points, C = 70-79%/700-799 points, D = 60-69%/600-699 points While a D is a passing grade, all students should strive to earn a C or higher in this required course. Course Policies: Attendance Students will be asked to sign an attendance sheet at the beginning of each class session. If a student forgets to sign the attendance sheet, or arrive after the instructor collects the sheet, they will be counted as absent from that class period. It is the student’s responsibility to sign the attendance sheet. Attendance is expected of all students. A total of two excused absences are permitted in this course. Use absences wisely. Any student with three will automatically be deducted 50% of their Attendance grade. Four plus absences results in a 0% for their Attendance grade. These excused absences should cover the usual ailments: flu, sleeping in, the dog ate my homework, etc. If students have a serious illness or family emergency that would keep them from the course for more than three class periods, please consult with the instructor. Students with more than six absences should strongly consider dropping the course. Members of University of Idaho teams or organizations who will be absent from class for school-sponsored activities during the semester should inform the instructor of these absences in writing prior to the event. If the instructor does not receive notice of the event prior to the missed class period, the day missed will be counted as an unexcused absence. Students must check with the instructor to see if they need to make up any in-class or homework assignments. All makeup work for excused absences must be completed within a calendar week of the absence (tests must be made up prior). Contacting the Professor Office hours are listed at the top of this syllabus. Please utilize these opportunities to meet with the instructor if you are having difficulty with a concept from class, find a reading challenging, or wish to ask specific questions about your grade or an ongoing assignment. Additionally, when emailing me please include a salutation and signature, (Professor, and –Tom) would suffice. Emails should contain complete information especially if it pertains to late materials, missing class, etc. “Hey, I missed class the other week because I was sick, can I make stuff up?” would be an example of inappropriate correspondence. A more appropriate correspondence would be “Hello Professor, I missed class last Wednesday, October 3rd, because I was sick with strep throat. What do I need to do to catch up in the course? Thank you –Jane.” Academic Integrity Instructors and students are responsible for maintaining academic standards and integrity in their classes. Consequences for academic dishonesty may be imposed by the course instructor at their discretion. Such academic consequences may include but cannot exceed a grade of “F” in the course. If the student deems the grade unfair, he or she may appeal through the appropriate departmental administrator and college dean, and finally to the Academic Hearing Board. In addition to the academic consequences, disciplinary penalties for academic dishonesty may include suspension or expulsion and must be handled by the Student Judicial System, which is described in the Student Code of Conduct section of the “Policies & Information of Interest to Students” booklet and the Faculty-Staff Handbook. Of special note, use of assignment or text banks will be pursued definitively as academic dishonesty. DO NOT USE ASSIGNMENT BANKS. Misc. Course Policies The instructor does not allow unauthorized video or audio recordings of class lectures due to intellectual property concerns. If you wish to make recordings, please talk with the instructor privately before doing so. NO CELL PHONES are allowed out during class. Laptops are permitted if the student sits in the front two rows of class. If students use their computer to engage in social media, streaming videos, online shopping, or other non-course related items, they will receive a letter grade deduction per offense in their Homework/In-Class Activity grade. The instructor does not post lecture notes online. Students are responsible for collecting notes from classmates if they miss a class for any reason (including a University of Idaho excused absence). The instructor does not provide lecture notes unless it is a remarkable circumstance and/or emergency. Reasonable accommodations are available for students who have documented temporary or permanent disabilities. All accommodations must be approved through the Center for Disability Access and Resources located in the Bruce M. Pitman Center, Suite 127 in order to notify your instructor(s) as soon as possible regarding accommodation(s) needed for the course. The instructor reserves the right to make changes in assignments, testing procedures and course policies that are in the students’ best interests.
